newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak govt, opponents trade blame on referendums.
newsitem.headline: Slovak govt, opponents trade blame on referendums.

text.p: Voting in Slovak referendums, seen as a vital test of democracy, ended in chaos on Saturday after a widespread boycott and the government and opposition trading blame for the failure.

A feud between President Michal Kovac and Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar led to a question on whether the people and not the parliament should elect the president being struck off ballot papers at the last minute.
The remaining three questions, asking whether Slovakia supported NATO membership, became almost irrelevant.
Foreign diplomats regarded the referendums as a key test of democracy in Slovakia, which has said it wants to be integrated with Western structures, including NATO and the European Union.
Ahead of results expected on Sunday afternoon, government and opposition leaders acknowledged that the turnout was low and threatened each other with legal action.
"The referendum was thwarted by the government and premier Meciar," opposition Christian Democratic Movement leader Ivan Simko told a joint opposition news conference.
But parliamentary chairman Ivan Gasparovic, of Meciar's Movement for a Democratic Slovakia (HZDS), accused Kovac and the opposition of causing the confusion.
"The president also contributed to the failure of the referendum," he told Slovak television. "He indirectly called on the population to boycott the referendum before it was held."
Kovac, who had called on voters to support both NATO membership and direct presidential elections, then refused to vote himself and urged others to do the same.
The proposal to have the president elected directly had been framed by those who want to prevent Meciar from assuming presidential powers when Kovac's term ends next March.
Interior Minister Gustav Krajci removed the question, insisting it was illegal, despite a Central Referendum Committee (UKR) ruling that it should be included.
"I regret this chaos around the referendum, but those who wanted to say yes to NATO membership could do it despite the absence of the fourth question," he told Slovak television.
The opposition and the referendum committee both threatened legal action against Krajci, who said mayors who refused to accept the three-question ballot papers could face charges.
A referendum committee official said it had received 150 official complaints from all over Slovakia.
Many polling stations reported a preliminary turnout of no more than 15 percent. By law a referendum needs a turnout of more than 50 percent to be valid.
"It is a defeat for Meciar's ruling coalition, as they did not get to vote even all of their own supporters," said Bela Bugar of the ethnic-Hungarian Christian Democrats.
In the 1994 general elections, Meciar's HZDS received around 35 percent of the votes.

Opposition leaders said they would take "any possible moves" to force through the change in the law on presidential elections. The dispute springs from a clause in the constitution requiring a three-fifths majority in parliament to elect the president.

If no candidate can muster a sufficient margin, as seems likely given the present strengths of the parties, presidential powers would pass to the prime minister, a provision the present prime minister has fought to keep.
